column5: The register set for each remapping hardware unit is placed at a size-aligned memory-mapped location whose exact position is implementation-dependent and is communicated to system software by BIOS through the ACPI DMA-remapping hardware reporting structures.
Hardware implementations that support relocating the remapping registers in the system address map must provide the ability to lock their location by hardware-specific secure initialization software.

Software is expected to access 32-bit remapping registers as aligned doublewords, and must access 64-bit and 128-bit registers as either aligned quadwords or aligned doublewords; hardware may disassemble a quadword access into two doubleword accesses and must then complete them in order, lower doubleword first.
Locked operations to remapping hardware registers are not supported and software must not issue them.

The attribute identifying the originator of an I/O transaction is called the source-id; for PCI Express devices the source-id is the requester identifier in the transaction layer header, composed of the device's PCI Bus, Device and Function number.
In the requester-id format the Bus number occupies bits 15:8, the Device number bits 7:3, and the Function number bits 2:0.
For PCI Express devices supporting Alternative Routing-ID Interpretation (ARI), the bits traditionally used for the Device Number field are instead used to expand the Function Number field.
For root-complex integrated devices the source-id may be derived from the root-complex internal implementation rather than carried in the transaction.

Chapter 3 of the VT-d specification is titled "DMA Remapping" and defines domains and address translation in §3.2, legacy mode address translation in §3.4.2 and scalable mode address translation in §3.4.3.
The mode a remapping hardware unit operates in is selected by the Translation Table Mode (TTM) field, bits 11:10 of the Root Table Address Register.
RTADDR_REG.TTM = 00b selects legacy mode and RTADDR_REG.TTM = 01b selects scalable mode.

RTADDR_REG.TTM programmed to 11b selects Abort DMA Mode on hardware reporting ADMS = 1 in the Extended Capability Register; programming 11b where ADMS = 0, or programming 10b at all, is a fault condition.
RTADDR_REG bit 7 is SSIRWE (Second Stage I/O Read/Write Enable) and bits 63:12 are RTA, the root-table address.
Setting RTADDR_REG.SSIRWE while TTM is programmed to legacy mode (00b) is an invalid programming fault condition.
Rev 5.20 names the translation stages "First-Stage Translation" (§3.6) and "Second-Stage Translation" (§3.7), with nested translation in §3.8 and pass-through translation in §3.9.
A root-entry is 128 bits: bit 0 is Present (P), bits 11:1 are reserved, bits 63:12 are the Context-table Pointer (CTP) and bits 127:64 are reserved.
The context-table referenced by a root-entry CTP is 4 KB in size and size-aligned, and hardware treats CTP bits 63:HAW as reserved where HAW is the platform host address width.
The Root Table Address Register points at a table of root-entries when its TTM field is 00b.
A scalable-mode root-entry has LP (Lower Present) at bit 0, LCTP (Lower Context Table Pointer) at bits 63:12, UP (Upper Present) at bit 64 and UCTP (Upper Context Table Pointer) at bits 127:76.
Both the upper and lower scalable-mode context-tables are 4 KB in size and size-aligned, and the Root Table Address Register points at a table of scalable-mode root-entries when TTM is 01b.

A context-entry has P at bit 0, FPD at bit 1, TT (Translation Type) at bits 3:2, SSPTPTR at bits 63:12, AW (Address Width) at bits 66:64, ignored bits at 70:67, and DID (Domain Identifier) at bits 87:72.
Context-entry AW encodings are 000b reserved, 001b = 39-bit AGAW (3-level page table), 010b = 48-bit AGAW (4-level), 011b = 57-bit AGAW (5-level), and 100b–111b reserved.

Context-entry TT encodings are 00b (untranslated requests translated through SSPTPTR; translated and translation requests blocked), 01b (untranslated, translated and translation requests supported, reserved when ECAP.DT = 0), 10b (untranslated requests processed as pass-through, SSPTPTR ignored, reserved when ECAP.PT = 0) and 11b reserved.
The context-entry TT field applies only to requests-without-PASID, because hardware blocks all requests-with-PASID in legacy mode before they can use the context table.
When context-entry TT indicates pass-through (10b), the AW field must be programmed to the largest AGAW value supported by hardware.
Context-entries programmed with the same domain identifier must always reference the same address translation through SSPTPTR.
When the Caching Mode (CM) field in the Capability Register is Set, the domain-id value of zero is architecturally reserved and software must not use it.
The FPD field is evaluated by hardware irrespective of the setting of the Present field, so a not-present entry can still suppress fault reporting.

A scalable-mode context-entry is 256 bits with P at bit 0, FPD at bit 1, DTE at bit 2, PASIDE at bit 3, PRE at bit 4, HPTE at bit 5, EPTR at bit 6, PDTS at bits 11:9, PASIDDIRPTR at bits 63:12, RID_PASID at bits 83:64 and RID_PRIV at bit 84.
A value of X in the PDTS field indicates that the scalable-mode PASID-directory has 2^(X+7) entries.
Requests-without-PASID processed through a scalable-mode context-entry are treated as requests-with-PASID whose PASID value is taken from the RID_PASID field, with ExecuteRequested treated as 0.
RID_PASID is treated as Reserved(0) on implementations reporting RPS = 0 in the Extended Capability Register, and such implementations use a PASID value of 0 for requests-without-PASID.
RID_PRIV is treated as Reserved(0) on implementations reporting RPRIVS = 0 in the Extended Capability Register, which then use a PrivilegeModeRequested value of 0 for requests-without-PASID.

DTE = 0 blocks translation requests (with or without PASID) and translated requests received through that scalable-mode context-entry; DTE = 1 allows translation requests to be processed through the PASID structures while translated requests bypass address translation.
PRE is treated as Reserved(0) where ECAP.PRS = 0; when Clear, page requests reporting recoverable address translation faults are blocked.
PASIDE is treated as Reserved(0) where ECAP.PASID = 0; when Clear, requests-with-PASID received through that scalable-mode context-entry are blocked. PASIDE does not apply to requests-without-PASID.
EPTR is treated as Reserved(0) where ECAP.PTRS = 0; when Clear, translated requests with PASID are treated as Unsupported Request.
HPTE is treated as Reserved(0) where ECAP.HPTS = 0; when Set, processing of translated requests includes the Host Permission Table.
Programming DTE = 0 together with PRE = 1 in a scalable-mode context-entry is an illegal combination and raises a fault.
A scalable-mode PASID-directory entry has P at bit 0, FPD at bit 1, reserved bits 11:2, and SMPTBLPTR at bits 63:12 pointing at the base of a 4 KB scalable-mode PASID-table.
SMPTBLPTR is always treated as a Host Physical Address, with bits 63:HAW reserved.
If a scalable-mode PASID-directory entry is referenced through a scalable-mode context-entry whose FPD field is 1, the directory entry's own FPD field has no effect.
A scalable-mode PASID-table entry is 512 bits wide.

In a scalable-mode PASID-table entry, P is bit 0, FPD is bit 1, AW is bits 4:2, PGTT is bits 8:6, SSADE is bit 9 and DID is bits 79:64; unlike the root, context and PASID-directory entries, the §9.6 bit table states the pointer bounds in terms of HAW, giving SSPTPTR as bits (HAW-1):12 with bits 63:HAW Reserved.

In a scalable-mode PASID-table entry, PWSNP is bit 87, PGSNP is bit 88, PAT is bits 127:96, SRE is bit 128, FSPM is bits 131:130, WPE is bit 132, EAFE is bit 135, and FSPTPTR is bits (HAW+127):140 with bits 191:(HAW+128) Reserved.

PGTT encodings 000b, 101b, 110b and 111b are invalid; PGTT = 001b requires ECAP_REG.FSTS to be Set and PGTT = 010b requires the corresponding second-stage support bit, otherwise the entry is treated as invalidly programmed.
PGTT = 011b selects nested translation, in which the FSPTPTR of a present scalable-mode PASID-table entry is itself translated through the second stage.
PGTT = 100b selects pass-through translation.
SSADE controls whether Accessed and Dirty flags are enabled in second-stage paging entries; when SSADE = 0 the A and D bits in second-stage entries are ignored by hardware.
A scalable-mode PASID-table entry whose SRE field is 0 blocks untranslated and translation requests carrying a Set Privileged-mode-Requested field.

In a first-stage PTE mapping a 4-KByte page, P is bit 0, R/W bit 1, U/S bit 2, PWT bit 3, PCD bit 4, A bit 5, D bit 6, PAT bit 7, G bit 8, EA bit 10, ADDR bits (HAW-1):12, bits 51:HAW reserved and bits 63:52 ignored.
Hardware ignores the G (Global) bit in first-stage paging entries and functions as if it were Clear.
The Extended Accessed (EA) bit at position 10 is meaningful only when EAFE = 1 in the relevant scalable-mode PASID-table entry, and is otherwise ignored.
In first-stage paging entries, bit 7 is PS (Page Size) for PDPE and PDE entries — must be 1 to map a 1-GByte or 2-MByte page respectively, and 0 to reference the next-level table.
The ADDR field of a first-stage paging entry is treated as a Guest Physical Address when the PGTT field in the relevant scalable-mode PASID-table entry is programmed as nested (011b).
Reserved bits 29:13 in a first-stage PDPE mapping a 1-GByte page, and bits 20:13 in a PDE mapping a 2-MByte page, must be zero.
In a second-stage PTE mapping a 4-KByte page, R is bit 0, W is bit 1, EMT is bits 5:3, IPAT is bit 6, A is bit 8, D is bit 9, SNP is bit 11, ADDR is bits (HAW-1):12, IR is bit 61 and IW is bit 62.
In second-stage SS-PDPE and SS-PDE entries, bit 7 is PS (Page Size): 1 maps a 1-GByte or 2-MByte page respectively, 0 references the next-level second-stage table.
The SNP field at bit 11 indicates whether accesses to the page must snoop processor caches, and is treated as reserved(0) on implementations reporting SC = 0 in the Extended Capability Register.

When Second Stage I/O Read/Write bits are not enabled the two bits are treated asymmetrically: IW (bit 62) is treated as Reserved(0) while IR (bit 61) is merely ignored. When they are enabled, IW = 0 denies write permission and IR = 0 denies read permission for the region controlled by the entry.

IPAT and EMT are ignored by hardware when the Extended Memory Type Enable (EMTE) field is Clear in the relevant scalable-mode PASID-table entry or when the Translation Table Mode is legacy (TTM = 00b).
Second-stage A and D bits at positions 8 and 9 are ignored by hardware when SSADE = 0 in the relevant scalable-mode PASID-table entry.
In second-stage paging entries the address field is a Host Physical Address; in the 1-GByte and 2-MByte page-mapping forms, reserved fields 29:12 and 20:12 respectively must be zero.
In the remapping register region, VER_REG is at 000h, CAP_REG at 008h, ECAP_REG at 010h, GCMD_REG at 018h, GSTS_REG at 01Ch, RTADDR_REG at 020h and CCMD_REG at 028h.
FSTS_REG is at 034h, the Fault Event Control Register at 038h, Fault Event Data at 03Ch, Fault Event Address at 040h and Fault Event Upper Address at 044h.
The Protected Memory Enable Register is at 064h, Protected Low-Memory Base at 068h, Protected Low-Memory Limit at 06Ch, Protected High-Memory Base at 070h and Protected High-Memory Limit at 078h.

The Invalidation Queue Head is at 080h, Invalidation Queue Tail at 088h, Invalidation Queue Address Register at 090h, Invalidation Completion Status Register at 09Ch and the Invalidation Queue Error Record Register at 0B0h.
The Invalidation Completion Event Control, Data, Address and Upper Address registers are at 0A0h, 0A4h, 0A8h and 0ACh respectively.
The Interrupt Remapping Table Address Register is at 0B8h.
The Page Request Queue Head, Tail and Address registers are at 0C0h, 0C8h and 0D0h, the Page Request Status Register at 0DCh and the Page Request Event Control Register at 0E0h.
The MTRR Capability Register is at 100h and the MTRR Default Type Register at 108h.

The Performance Monitoring Capability Register is at 300h, the Enhanced Command Register at 400h, the RDT Configuration Register at DC0h, the Virtual Command Register at E00h and the Virtual Command Capability Register at E30h.

Hardware may place the IOTLB registers and fault recording registers at any unused or reserved address in the 4 KB register space or in adjoined 4 KB regions; software must read the Capability Register to determine their offsets.

In CAP_REG, ND is bits 2:0, RWBF bit 4, PLMR bit 5, PHMR bit 6, CM bit 7, SAGAW bits 12:8, MGAW bits 21:16, ZLR bit 22, FRO bits 33:24, SSLPS bits 37:34, PSI bit 39, NFR bits 47:40, MAMV bits 53:48, DWD bit 54, DRD bit 55, FS1GP bit 56, PI bit 59, FS5LP bit 60, ECMDS bit 61, ESIRTPS bit 62 and ESRTPS bit 63.

In Rev 5.20 CAP_REG bit 3 is plain **Reserved (RsvdZ)** while **only bit 23 carries the DEP "Deprecated" marking**; both read as 0. The distinction matters when reading the register table — bit 3 lost the advanced-fault-logging capability outright rather than being deprecated in place.

CAP_REG.ND encodes domain-id width: 000b = 4-bit (16 domains), 001b = 6-bit (64), 010b = 8-bit (256), 011b = 10-bit (1024), 100b = 12-bit (4K), 101b = 14-bit (16K), 110b = 16-bit (64K) and 111b reserved — which is why the DID fields in the context-entry and the scalable-mode PASID-table entry are 16 bits wide.
The Maximum Guest Address Width is computed as N+1 where N is the value in CAP_REG.MGAW; an implementation supporting 48-bit MGAW reports 47 (101111b).
CAP_REG.SSLPS bit 0 indicates support for a 21-bit offset to page frame (2 MB) and bit 1 a 30-bit offset (1 GB); bits 2 and 3 are reserved.
If the register base address is X and CAP_REG.FRO reports Y, the address of the first fault recording register is X + (16 * Y).
The number of fault recording registers is N+1 where N is CAP_REG.NFR; implementations must support at least one per remapping hardware unit and the maximum is 256.
CAP_REG.MAMV gives the maximum supported value for the Address Mask field in IVA_REG and in the IOTLB Invalidation Descriptor, and is valid only when CAP_REG.PSI is Set.

In ECAP_REG, C is bit 0, QI bit 1, DT bit 2, IR bit 3, EIM bit 4, PT bit 6, SC bit 7, IRO bits 17:8, MHMV bits 23:20, MTS bit 25, NEST bit 26, PRS bit 29, ERS bit 30, SRS bit 31, NWFS bit 33, EAFS bit 34 and PSS bits 39:35.

In ECAP_REG, PASID is bit 40, DIT bit 41, PDS bit 42, SMTS bit 43, VCS bit 44, SSADS bit 45, SSTS bit 46, FSTS bit 47, SMPWCS bit 48, RPS bit 49, TDXCS bit 50, PMS bit 51, ADMS bit 52, RPRIVS bit 53, HPTS bit 55, PTRS bit 56, SSIRWS bit 57, SMS bit 58, HPT1GPS bit 59, RDTS bit 60, EIMER bit 61 and IRREQ bit 62.
ECAP_REG bits 5, 24 and 28 are marked Deprecated in Rev 5.20 and must be reported as 0.
If the register base address is X and ECAP_REG.IRO reports Y, the IOTLB registers are at X + (16 * Y).
ECAP_REG.SC = 1 means hardware supports the 1-setting of the SNP field in second-stage page-table entries and the PGSNP field in scalable-mode PASID-table entries.
ECAP_REG.MHMV reports the maximum supported value for the Interrupt Mask field in the Interrupt Entry Cache Invalidation Descriptor, and reads as 0 when IR is Clear.
ECAP_REG.EIM = 1 indicates hardware supports 32-bit APIC-IDs (x2APIC mode); implementations reporting IR as Clear also report EIM as Clear.
In GCMD_REG, TE is bit 31, SRTP bit 30, WBF bit 27, QIE bit 26, IRE bit 25, SIRTP bit 24 and CFI bit 23; bits 29:28 and 22:0 are reserved in Rev 5.20.
GSTS_REG mirrors GCMD_REG with TES at bit 31, RTPS bit 30, WBFS bit 27, QIES bit 26, IRES bit 25, IRTPS bit 24 and CFIS bit 23; bits 29:28 and 22:0 are reserved.
All GCMD_REG command fields are write-only; software reads the corresponding GSTS_REG field to observe the result.
If multiple control fields in GCMD_REG need to be modified, software must serialize the modifications through multiple writes to the register.

To update GCMD_REG bit X to value Y, software reads GSTS_REG, masks the result with 96FFFFFFh to reset the one-shot bits, sets or clears bit X, writes the result to GCMD_REG, and waits until GSTS_REG[X] indicates the command is serviced.
Behaviour is undefined if GCMD_REG is written while a command is in progress on the Enhanced Command Interface (ECRESP_REG.IP = 1).
Hardware must enable or disable remapping logic only at deterministic transaction boundaries, so that an in-flight transaction is either subject to remapping or not at all.
Set Root Table Pointer operation is specified in VT-d §6.6, Set Interrupt Remapping Table Pointer operation in §6.7 and Write Buffer Flushing in §6.8.
In the Protected Memory Enable Register, EPM (Enable Protected Memory) is bit 31 and PRS (Protected Region Status) is bit 0.

The protected low-memory region is described by the Protected Low-Memory Base and Limit registers (§11.4.8.2 and §11.4.8.3) and the protected high-memory region by the Protected High-Memory Base and Limit registers (§11.4.8.4 and §11.4.8.5).
Support for the protected low- and high-memory regions is reported by CAP_REG.PLMR (bit 5) and CAP_REG.PHMR (bit 6).

VT-d Chapter 6 defines the context-cache (§6.2.2), PASID-cache (§6.2.3), IOTLB (§6.2.4), paging-structure caches PML5-cache / PML4-cache / PDPE-cache / PDE-cache (§6.2.5), HPT cache (§6.2.6) and interrupt entry cache (§6.4).
The Caching Mode field in the Capability Register indicates whether the hardware implementation caches not-present or erroneous translation-structure entries.

When CM is Set, any software update to remapping structures other than first-stage mappings, including updates to not-present entries and to present entries whose programming resulted in translation faults, requires explicit invalidation of the caches.

Hardware implementations of the architecture must support operation corresponding to CM = 0; CM = 1 exists so that software emulating remapping hardware can virtualize it efficiently, and software managing remapping hardware should handle both caching modes.

In CCMD_REG, ICC (Invalidate Context-Cache) is bit 63, CIRG (Context Invalidation Request Granularity) bits 62:61, CAIG (Context Actual Invalidation Granularity) bits 60:59, FM (Function Mask) bits 33:32, SID bits 31:16 and DID bits 15:0.
CCMD_REG.CIRG encodes global invalidation as 01b, domain-selective invalidation as 10b and device-selective invalidation as 11b.

The IOTLB registers consist of two adjacently placed 64-bit registers: the Invalidate Address Register at the offset reported by ECAP_REG.IRO, and the IOTLB Invalidate Register at that offset plus 008h.

In the IOTLB Invalidate Register, IVT (Invalidate IOTLB) is bit 63, IIRG (IOTLB Invalidation Request Granularity) bits 61:60, IAIG (IOTLB Actual Invalidation Granularity) bits 58:57, DR (Drain Reads) bit 49, DW (Drain Writes) bit 48 and DID bits 47:32.
In the Invalidate Address Register, ADDR is bits 63:12, IH (Invalidation Hint) is bit 6 and AM (Address Mask) is bits 5:0.
Page-selective invalidation through IVA_REG is available only on hardware reporting CAP_REG.PSI as Set.
Queued invalidation is supported only on hardware reporting ECAP_REG.QI as Set, is enabled through GCMD_REG.QIE and observed through GSTS_REG.QIES.
The invalidation queue is located by IQA_REG at offset 090h, with IQH_REG at 080h giving the offset of the descriptor hardware will read next and IQT_REG at 088h the offset software will write next.
The Type field of an invalidation descriptor is a 7-bit field formed by concatenating bits 11:9 and bits 3:0 of the descriptor.

Invalidation descriptor type 1h is the Context-cache Invalidate Descriptor, 2h the IOTLB Invalidate Descriptor, 3h the Device-TLB Invalidate Descriptor, 4h the Interrupt Entry Cache Invalidate Descriptor and 5h the Invalidation Wait Descriptor.

Invalidation descriptor type 6h is the PASID-based IOTLB Invalidate Descriptor, 7h the PASID-cache Invalidate Descriptor, 8h the PASID-based-Device-TLB Invalidate Descriptor and Ah the HPT Cache Invalidate Descriptor.
The Page Group Response Descriptor, submitted through the invalidation queue, carries Type value 9h.

One rule covers both IOTLB forms: hardware executes an IOTLB invalidation descriptor (`iotlb_inv_dsc`) or a PASID-based IOTLB invalidation descriptor (`p_iotlb_inv_dsc`) only after all context-cache *and* PASID-cache invalidation descriptors ahead of it in the invalidation queue are completed.

Hardware executes a PASID-cache invalidation descriptor only after all context-cache invalidation descriptors ahead of it in the invalidation queue are completed, and executes a Device-TLB invalidation descriptor only after all IOTLB and Interrupt Entry Cache invalidation descriptors ahead of it are completed.
Software must always request IOTLB invalidation before requesting the corresponding Device-TLB invalidation.
If the Fence (FN) flag is 1 in an Invalidation Wait Descriptor, hardware must execute descriptors following it only after the wait command is completed.

The Invalidation Wait Descriptor allows software to synchronize with hardware for descriptors submitted ahead of it, and hardware generation of invalidation completion events is specified in §6.5.2.10.
When the Invalidation Time-out Error (ITE) condition is signalled, hardware aborts any Invalidation Wait Descriptor commands pending in hardware.
VT-d §6.5.3.3 gives normative guidance to software for invalidations, and §6.5.3.4 the equivalent guidance when HPT is enabled.
Draining of requests to memory is specified in §6.5.4 and interrupt draining in §6.5.5.

VT-d Chapter 4 "Support For Device-TLBs" defines Device-TLB operation in §4.1, comprising translation requests (§4.1.1), translation completions (§4.1.2), translated requests (§4.1.3) and invalidation requests and completions (§4.1.4).
Device-TLB support is enumerated by ECAP_REG.DT (bit 2), and in legacy mode is enabled per device by the context-entry TT field value 01b.
In scalable mode, device-TLB use is gated by the DTE field at bit 2 of the scalable-mode context-entry.
VT-d §4.5 gives recommended software sequences to enable ATS (§4.5.1) and to disable ATS (§4.5.2).
Handling of ATS protocol errors is specified in §4.2.1, root-port control of ATS address types in §4.2.2, and handling of translation requests in §4.2.3.
Device TLBs in System-on-Chip integrated devices are treated separately in §4.4.

The Host Permission Table — a permission structure consulted when processing translated requests — is specified in §4.2.4, with its entry formats HPTL4E through HPTL1E in §9.12. It was added in **Rev 5.0** (August 2024), not Rev 5.20; Rev 5.20's only HPT change was making some §7.1.3 fault conditions Not Applicable when HPT is disabled.
Page Request Service support is enumerated by ECAP_REG.PRS (bit 29) and enabled per device by the PRE field at bit 4 of the scalable-mode context-entry.
PASID support is enumerated by ECAP_REG.PASID (bit 40), and the supported PASID width is reported by ECAP_REG.PSS at bits 39:35.
The PASID field in a scalable-mode context-entry's RID_PASID occupies 20 bits (83:64), consistent with the 20-bit PASID space.
Supervisor Request support is enumerated by ECAP_REG.SRS (bit 31) and Execute Request support by ECAP_REG.ERS (bit 30).

A request-with-PASID carrying a Set Execute-Requested (ER) field is a fault condition **unconditionally** on hardware reporting Major Version 8 and above in VER_REG — there is no configuration that permits it — and on Major Version 7 and below it is a fault only when ECAP_REG.ERS is 0. ERS itself is reported as Clear by every conforming implementation, being planned for deprecation.
VT-d §3.12.7 explicitly covers Intel Scalable I/O Virtualization capable devices as a category of DMA request origination, alongside SR-IOV capable devices in §3.12.6.

Requests crossing page boundaries are handled per §3.13, zero-length reads per §3.14, requests to the interrupt address range per §3.15, requests to reserved system memory per §3.16, and root-complex peer-to-peer considerations per §3.17.
Hardware detecting an output address in the interrupt address range FEEx_xxxxh after remapping raises a fault in both legacy mode and scalable mode.
Snoop behaviour is specified in §3.10 and memory type in §3.11, with the effective memory type derivation in §3.11.3 and the mode-specific rules in §3.11.4.1 (legacy) and §3.11.4.2 (scalable).
Appendix A of the VT-d specification tabulates snoop and memory type for the various remapping structures.
VT-d Chapter 5 is titled "Interrupt Remapping" and covers interrupt remapping in §5.1 and interrupt posting in §5.2.
Interrupt-remapping support is enumerated by the IR field at bit 3 of the Extended Capability Register.
The VT-d specification identifies interrupt isolation, interrupt migration and x2APIC support as the three motivations for hardware interrupt remapping.
To support domain-isolation usages, platform hardware must be capable of uniquely identifying the requester (source-id) for each interrupt message.
For message-signaled interrupt requests from PCI Express devices and from root-complex integrated PCI or PCI Express devices, the source-id is the device's PCI requester-id.

For message-signaled interrupt requests from devices behind PCI Express-to-PCI/PCI-X bridges, the requester identifier may be that of the interrupting device or the bridge's secondary-interface bus number with device and function number zero; because of this aliasing, interrupt-remapping hardware does not isolate interrupts from individual devices behind such bridges.

For message-signaled interrupt requests from devices behind conventional PCI bridges the source-id is the requester-id of the legacy bridge device, so interrupt-remapping hardware does not isolate such requests from individual devices either.

For devices using legacy interrupt routing the I/OxAPIC generates the interrupt-request transaction, and interrupt-remapping hardware requires each I/OxAPIC in the platform to include a unique 16-bit source-id in its requests, reported by BIOS through ACPI structures.

Other platform devices that are not PCI discoverable yet can generate message-signaled interrupts, such as integrated High Precision Event Timer devices, must be assigned unique non-conflicting 16-bit source-ids reported by BIOS through ACPI structures.
The Interrupt Format field is address bit 4; it is Clear for compatibility-format interrupt requests and Set for remappable-format interrupt requests.
Compatibility-format interrupt requests are specified in VT-d §5.1.2.1 and remappable-format requests in §5.1.2.2.
Compatibility-format interrupts are blocked when Extended Interrupt Mode is enabled (IRTA_REG.EIME Set) or when compatibility-format interrupts are disabled (GSTS_REG.CFIS Clear).
In the remappable interrupt-request format, address bits 31:20 are the Interrupt Identifier and a DWORD DMA write with FEEh in those bits is decoded as an interrupt request by the root complex.

In the remappable format, address bits 19:5 carry Handle[14:0], bit 4 is the Interrupt Format field (1b), bit 3 is SubHandle Valid (SHV), bit 2 carries Handle[15], and bits 1:0 are ignored by interrupt-remapping hardware.
The 16-bit Handle provides 64K unique interrupt requests per remapping hardware unit.
SHV specifies whether the interrupt request payload contains a valid Subhandle, which enables MSI constructs supporting only a single address with multiple data values.
When SHV is Set, data bits 15:0 contain the 16-bit Subhandle and data bits 31:16 are treated as reserved (0); when SHV is Clear the whole data field is ignored by hardware.

Interrupt-remapping hardware uses a memory-resident single-level table called the Interrupt Remapping Table, whose base address and size are specified through the Interrupt Remap Table Address Register.
Each entry in the interrupt remapping table is 128 bits in size and is called an Interrupt Remapping Table Entry (IRTE).
The maximum number of IRTEs in an interrupt remapping table is 64K.
For remappable-format requests, hardware computes interrupt_index as address.handle when address.SHV is 0, and as address.handle + data.subhandle when SHV is 1.
If the computed interrupt_index is equal to or larger than the number of IRTEs in the remapping table, hardware treats the interrupt request as an error.
Remapping hardware units in a platform may be configured to share an interrupt-remapping table or to use independent tables.
IRTA_REG lives at register offset 0B8h, with IRTA at bits 63:12, EIME at bit 11, reserved bits 10:4 and S (Size) at bits 3:0.
The number of entries in the interrupt remapping table is 2^(X+1), where X is the value programmed in IRTA_REG.S.
The IRTA field points to the base of a 4 KB-aligned interrupt remapping table, and hardware may ignore bits 63:HAW.
Values written to IRTA_REG take effect only after software executes the Set Interrupt Remap Table Pointer command.
IRTA_REG is treated as RsvdZ by implementations reporting Interrupt Remapping as not supported in the Extended Capability Register.

In the IRTE for remapped interrupts, P is bit 0, FPD bit 1, DM (Destination Mode) bit 2, RH (Redirection Hint) bit 3, TM (Trigger Mode) bit 4, DLM (Delivery Mode) bits 7:5, AVAIL bits 11:8, reserved bits 14:12, IM (IRTE Mode) bit 15, V (Vector) bits 23:16, reserved bits 31:24 and DST (Destination ID) bits 63:32.
In the IRTE for remapped interrupts, SID occupies bits 79:64, SQ bits 81:80, SVT bits 83:82 and bits 127:84 are reserved.
IM = 0 indicates that interrupt requests processed through the IRTE are remapped; IM = 1 indicates they are posted and the entry is interpreted in the posted format of §9.10.
The AVAIL field at bits 11:8 is available to software and hardware always ignores its programming.
The V field is an 8-bit field containing the interrupt vector associated with the remapped interrupt request, evaluated only when the Present field is Set.
The DST field identifies the remapped interrupt request's target processor or processors, and its interpretation depends on the interrupt-remapping mode in force.
RH indicates whether the remapped interrupt request should be directed to one among N processors specified in the Destination ID field, under hardware control.
DM indicates whether the Destination ID field should be interpreted as a logical or a physical APIC ID.
The 3-bit DLM field specifies how the remapped interrupt is handled, operates only in conjunction with specific Trigger Modes, and correct Trigger Modes must be guaranteed by software.

The all-zeros rule applies to SMI alone: for SMI (DLM = 010b) the vector field is ignored "but must be programmed to all zeros for future compatibility", whereas for NMI (100b) and INIT (101b) the specification says only that the vector information is ignored, with no zeroing requirement.

NMI, INIT and ExtINT are edge triggered regardless of the setting of the Trigger Mode field, and platforms supporting interrupt remapping are expected or recommended to generate SMI, NMI and INIT through a dedicated pin or platform-specific special messages.
The FPD field is evaluated by hardware irrespective of the setting of the Present field, while all other IRTE fields are evaluated only when P is Set.
When forwarding a remapped interrupt request to the system bus, the "Trigger Mode Level" field in the request on the system bus is always set to asserted (1b).
The SVT field specifies the type of validation interrupt-remapping hardware must perform on the source-id of interrupt requests referencing the IRTE, and is evaluated only when P is Set.

When SVT is 01b, the SID field specifies the requester-id allowed to originate interrupt requests referencing the IRTE, and the SQ field determines which bits of the SID field are considered in the verification.

When SVT is 10b, the upper 8 bits of the SID field contain a Startbus# and the lower 8 bits an Endbus#, and a referencing interrupt request must have a requester-id whose bus number lies within that range; this encoding may be used to verify interrupts originating behind PCI Express-to-PCI/PCI-X bridges.

The SQ field is evaluated by hardware only when the Present field is Set and the SVT field is 01b, and exists to verify origination of interrupt requests generated by devices supporting phantom functions.

The SQ encodings progressively ignore the least significant fields of the SID and requester-id: full comparison, comparison ignoring the third least significant field, comparison ignoring the second and third least significant fields, and comparison ignoring the least three significant fields.
The SID field is evaluated by hardware only when the Present field is Set and the SVT field is 01b or 10b.
In the IRTE for posted interrupts, P is bit 0, FPD bit 1, reserved bits 7:2, AVAIL bits 11:8, reserved bits 13:12, URG bit 14, IM bit 15, VV (Virtual Vector) bits 23:16 and reserved bits 37:24.

In the IRTE for posted interrupts, PDAL occupies bits 63:38 and specifies address bits 31:6 of the 64-byte aligned descriptor, SID bits 79:64, SQ bits 81:80, SVT bits 83:82, reserved bits 95:84 and PDAH bits 127:96 specifying address bits 63:32.
In the posted IRTE, hardware treats PDAH upper address bits 63:HAW as Reserved(0).

IM = 1 indicates interrupt requests processed through the IRTE are posted, and hardware implementations not supporting Posted Interrupts (PI = 0 in the Capability Register) treat the IM field as Reserved(0).

URG indicates whether the interrupt posted through the IRTE has latency-sensitive processing requirements, is evaluated only when both P and IM are Set, and is treated as Reserved(0) where PI = 0 in the Capability Register.

For posted-format IRTEs the vector field is the Virtual Vector and is used to determine which bit to Set when posting the interrupt, rather than to generate a remapped interrupt request as in remappable format.
Software is recommended to reserve a full cacheline to host the structure addressed by PDAL/PDAH for optimal performance.

Interrupt-posting capability is an extension of interrupt-remapping hardware that enables a remappable-format interrupt request to be posted in a coherent main-memory resident data structure, with an optional notification event to the CPU complex.
Remapping hardware support for interrupt posting is reported through the Posted Interrupt Support (PI) field at bit 59 of the Capability Register.

The IRTE Mode (IM) field alone decides whether a remappable interrupt request is subject to interrupt-remapping or interrupt-posting; all remappable requests are first processed through the Interrupt Remapping Table either way.

The structure that the posted IRTE addresses through PDAL/PDAH is 64-byte aligned and sized, must be allocated by system software in coherent write-back main memory, and its field semantics are owned by `07-apic-virtualization.md` — see that chapter, not this one.
When posting, hardware performs an atomic read-modify-write that always snoops processor caches irrespective of the value of the Page-walk Coherency (C) field in the Extended Capability Register.
Hardware implementations reporting Memory Type Support (MTS = 1 in ECAP_REG) must use the write-back memory type for the atomic operation that updates the posted structure.

During posting hardware claims exclusive ownership of the hosting cache-line, and if it detects invalid programming such as non-zero reserved fields it releases ownership and blocks the interrupt request.
After the atomic update, hardware promotes the cache-line to be globally observable before generating any notification event, and may write back the cache-line at any time after that step.
Interrupts generated by the remapping hardware itself are not subject to interrupt posting.
VT-d §5.2.5 is an informative section illustrating how VMM software may use interrupt-posting hardware for virtual-interrupt delivery; §5.2.6 covers interrupt posting for level-triggered interrupts.
Before an interrupt is posted and made visible to software, all preceding inbound DMA writes must be committed to their destinations.

An upstream read completion must wait until all preceding interrupts are completed, whether remapped or posted; for a posted interrupt, completion means both the atomic descriptor update and the associated notification event have completed.
Hardware must ensure the descriptor update is observable to software before issuing the notification event for that descriptor.
When IRTA_REG.EIME is 0, xAPIC mode is active and hardware interprets only bits 15:8 of the Destination-ID field in IRTEs, treating the high 16 bits and low 8 bits as reserved.
When IRTA_REG.EIME is 1, x2APIC mode is active and hardware interprets all 32 bits of the Destination-ID field in IRTEs.
EIME is implemented as RsvdZ on implementations reporting ECAP_REG.EIM as Clear.
Software must program EIME as Set on implementations reporting Extended Interrupt Mode Enable Required (EIMER) as Set in the Extended Capability Register.
Software must not modify EIME while interrupt remapping is active (GSTS_REG.IRES = 1).
If EIMER is reported Set and Extended Interrupt Mode is disabled, all interrupt requests are blocked.
Programming remapping hardware event interrupts differs between Intel 64 xAPIC mode (§5.1.6.1) and Intel 64 x2APIC mode (§5.1.6.2).
SIRTP is GCMD_REG bit 24 and its completion is reported by GSTS_REG.IRTPS at bit 24; IRE is GCMD_REG bit 25 and its status IRES is GSTS_REG bit 25.
CFI is GCMD_REG bit 23 and CFIS is GSTS_REG bit 23, controlling and reporting whether compatibility-format interrupts are permitted.
The Set Interrupt Remapping Table Pointer operation is specified in VT-d §6.7, and hardware reporting ESIRTPS (CAP_REG bit 62) performs an implicit invalidation as part of that operation.
The interrupt entry cache is described in VT-d §6.4 and is invalidated using the Interrupt Entry Cache Invalidate Descriptor, type 4h, specified in §6.5.2.8.
The maximum supported value for the Interrupt Mask (IM) field of the Interrupt Entry Cache Invalidate Descriptor is reported by ECAP_REG.MHMV at bits 23:20.
Interrupt draining is specified in VT-d §6.5.5.

Hardware decodes requests to the address range FEEx_xxxxh as interrupt requests, and when Interrupt Remapping Required is reported Set (ECAP_REG.IRREQ = 1) with interrupt remapping disabled, the interrupt request is blocked.
When ECAP_REG.IRREQ is Clear and interrupt remapping is not enabled, all interrupt requests are processed per the compatibility interrupt request format.

For a remappable-format request hardware performs reserved-field checking, retrieves Source-id, Handle, SHV and Subhandle, computes and bounds-checks interrupt_index, then obtains the IRTE from the Interrupt Entry Cache or fetches it from the interrupt-remapping table.
If ECAP_REG.C (Coherent) is reported Clear, IRTE fetches from memory do not snoop the processor caches.
Hardware must read the entire IRTE as a single operation and must not use multiple reads, because software may change the contents of the IRTE atomically.
Hardware implementations reporting MTS = 1 in ECAP_REG must use write-back memory type for IRTE fetches.
If the Present field in the IRTE is Clear, the interrupt request is blocked and treated as a fault; source-id checking per SVT, SID and SQ follows the presence check, and failure blocks the request.
Interrupt-remapping fault reason 20h is detection of one or more reserved fields Set when decoding the request per the remappable format, and is not a qualified fault.

Fault reason 21h covers an interrupt_index greater than the configured interrupt-remapping table size, or a hardware attempt to access the corresponding IRTE at an address above the Host Address Width.
Fault reason 22h is a Clear Present field in the IRTE corresponding to the interrupt_index.
Fault reason 23h is an error accessing the interrupt-remapping table through the IRTA field of IRTA_REG.
Fault reason 24h is detection of one or more reserved fields not initialized to zero in an IRTE with the Present field Set, including conditional reserved fields programmed wrongly.
Fault reason 25h is a blocked Compatibility-format interrupt request, either because EIME is Set in IRTA_REG or because CFIS is Clear in the Global Status Register.
Fault reason 26h is a blocked Remappable interrupt request due to verification failure of the requester's source-id against the SID, SVT and SQ fields of an IRTE with P Set.

Fault reasons 27h and 28h apply only to interrupt requests processed through IRTEs programmed for interrupt posting: 27h for an access error reaching the posted descriptor via the IRTE's address fields, 28h for non-zero reserved fields in that descriptor.
Fault reason 29h is an untranslated request-without-PASID to the interrupt address range FEEx_xxxxh that does not meet all the requirements to be considered a valid interrupt.
Fault reason 2Ah is an EIME value of 0 in IRTA_REG on an implementation reporting Extended Interrupt Mode Enable Required (EIMER) as Set in the Extended Capability Register.
Fault reason 2Bh is an MSI request received while Interrupt Remapping is disabled on remapping hardware reporting Interrupt Remapping Required (IRREQ) as Set in the Extended Capability Register.

An interrupt-remapping fault condition is treated as qualified if it is reported to software only when the Fault Processing Disable (FPD) field is Clear in the IRTE used to process the faulting request.
Interrupt translation faults are non-recoverable and the faulting interrupt request is treated as an Unsupported Request by the remapping hardware.
VT-d §5.1.5 specifies how to program interrupt sources to generate remappable interrupts, with I/OxAPIC programming in §5.1.5.1 and MSI/MSI-X register programming in §5.1.5.2.
In an I/OxAPIC Redirection Table Entry programmed for remapping, the most significant bit of the interrupt index, Interrupt_Index[15], is programmed in bit 11 of the RTE.
In the same RTE, Figure 5-3 places the Interrupt Format field (programmed to 1b) at bit 48 and Interrupt_Index[14:0] at bits 63:49, with the Vector remaining at bits 7:0.
The Trigger Mode field programmed in an I/OxAPIC RTE must match the Trigger Mode field in the IRTE it references, which is required for proper functioning of level-triggered interrupts.

For level-triggered interrupts, the Vector field programmed in the I/OxAPIC RTE must match the Vector field programmed in the referenced IRTE, which is required for correct processing of the End-Of-Interrupt broadcast by the I/OxAPIC.

To generate remappable interrupts from MSI or MSI-X, software programs address bits 31:20 with 0FEEh, sets the Interrupt Format field and the SHV field, and places Interrupt_Index[14:0] and Interrupt_Index[15] in the remaining address fields defined by the remappable format.
The Interrupt_Index programmed into an MSI or MSI-X address is the index of the IRTE that remaps the corresponding interrupt requests.
Devices supporting MSI allow software to enable multiple vectors, up to 32, in powers of two, which is why the Subhandle mechanism exists.
Programming of remapping hardware event interrupts is specified in VT-d §5.1.6, and handling of platform events in §5.1.7.
VT-d §5.3 summarizes memory type and snoop behaviour for interrupt-remapping structures.

The remappable interrupt format specifies only the fields needed to compute the interrupt_index; all other attributes of the remapped request come from the IRTE, which is what decouples interrupt attributes from the device programming.

The interrupt-remapping architecture defines hardware caching of frequently used IRTEs, and defines invalidation commands for the interrupt entry cache precisely so that software can update an IRTE dynamically.
